title: OA 2 — Building Skills (Easy to Medium)
description: Easy to Medium mock data-science internship assessment: CS/AI/ML/statistics/testing MCQs, aptitude, chart-based data analysis, SQL, pandas and DSA.
disclaimer: Independent practice material informed by publicly reported role requirements and general internship-assessment patterns. Not official Nasdaq questions.

revealPolicy.rule: Never send private fields to the candidate before the whole attempt has finished.

sections.title: Section 1: CS Fundamentals, AI, ML, Statistics and Testing

questions.statement: A model has high error on the training data and similarly high error on the test data. What is the most likely problem?

options.text: Underfitting: the model is too simple (high bias) to capture the pattern
Data leakage from the test set into the training set
The test set is too small to be used at all
Overfitting: the model has memorised the training data

solution.explanation: When both training and test errors are high and close together, the model lacks capacity (or features) to learn the pattern. Overfitting would show low training error and much higher test error.

hints: If even the training error is high, can the model be too complex?

questions.statement: A classifier produced TP = 40, TN = 45, FP = 5 and FN = 10 on 100 test cases. What is its accuracy?

solution.explanation: Accuracy = (TP + TN)/total = (40 + 45)/100 = 85%. 80% is the recall (40/50) and 88.9% is the precision (40/45), not the accuracy.

hints: Accuracy = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN).

questions.statement: A feature ranges from 10 to 50. After min–max scaling to [0, 1], what is the scaled value of 30?
hints: Min–max scaling: (x − min) / (max − min).

questions.statement: A fraud classifier scored 1,000 transactions and produced: TP = 30, FP = 20, FN = 10, TN = 940. What is its F1 score (to three decimals)?

solution.explanation: Precision = 30/(30+20) = 0.60 and recall = 30/(30+10) = 0.75, so F1 = 2·0.6·0.75/(0.6+0.75) = 0.667. 0.97 is accuracy ((30+940)/1000), which is dominated by the many true negatives; 0.60 and 0.75 are only the components.

hints: Precision = TP/(TP+FP), recall = TP/(TP+FN), F1 = 2PR/(P+R).

questions.statement: A linear regression has 200 correlated input features and the analyst wants an automatic feature subset where many coefficients are exactly zero. Which method is best suited?

options.text: Increasing the learning rate of the optimiser
L2-regularised regression (Ridge), which sets many coefficients exactly to zero
Ordinary least squares with no penalty

solution.explanation: The L1 penalty has a corner at zero and tends to drive some coefficients exactly to zero, giving sparsity. Ridge shrinks coefficients toward zero but rarely makes them exactly zero. OLS has no shrinkage; the learning rate affects optimisation, not the penalty.

hints: Which penalty (L1 or L2) can drive coefficients exactly to zero?

questions.statement: A logistic regression for card fraud has a coefficient of +0.69 on the feature 'number of foreign transactions in the last 24 h' (all other features held fixed). How is this coefficient best interpreted?

options.text: Each additional foreign transaction raises the probability of fraud by 0.69
The feature explains 69% of the variance in fraud
Each additional foreign transaction multiplies the probability of fraud by about 2
Each additional foreign transaction multiplies the odds of fraud by about 2 (e^0.69 ≈ 2)

solution.explanation: Logistic regression is linear in the log-odds, so a coefficient β multiplies the odds by e^β per unit increase. The effect on probability is not constant (it depends on the baseline), and the coefficient is not a variance-explained measure.

hints: Logistic regression is linear in the log-odds: odds multiply by e^β per unit.

questions.statement: A node has 50 fraud and 50 legitimate samples (Gini = 0.5). Split A sends 40 fraud + 10 legit left and 10 fraud + 40 legit right. Split B sends 30 fraud + 20 legit left and 20 fraud + 30 legit right. Which split does a Gini-based tree prefer?

options.text: Split B, because its children are larger and therefore more stable
Neither: both give the same impurity as the parent
Split B, with weighted child Gini 0.32
Split A, with weighted child Gini 0.32 versus 0.48 for split B

solution.explanation: Gini of a child = 1 − Σp². Split A children: 1 − (0.8² + 0.2²) = 0.32 each → weighted 0.32. Split B: 1 − (0.6² + 0.4²) = 0.48. The lower weighted impurity (larger impurity decrease) wins.

hints: Gini = 1 − Σp². Compute each child's Gini and weight by size; lower is better.

questions.statement: What is the median of the values 3, 9, 4, 7, 5, 8?

solution.explanation: Sorted: 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9. With six values the median is the average of the middle two: (5 + 7)/2 = 6. 5.5 and 7 are neighbouring values, not the median.

hints: Sort first. With an even count, average the two middle values.

questions.statement: Events A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.4. What is P(A and B)?

solution.explanation: For independent events P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B) = 0.3 × 0.4 = 0.12. 0.70 would be P(A) + P(B); 0.58 is P(A ∪ B).

hints: Independent events: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).

questions.statement: 2% of trades are fraudulent. A detector flags 90% of fraudulent trades and also flags 5% of legitimate trades. A randomly chosen trade is flagged. What is the probability that it is fraudulent?

solution.explanation: P(F|flag) = 0.02·0.90 / (0.02·0.90 + 0.98·0.05) = 0.018/0.067 ≈ 0.269. The base rate is low, so most flags are false alarms even with a good detector; 90% is the recall P(flag|F), not the posterior.

hints: Bayes: P(F|flag) = P(flag|F)P(F) / [P(flag|F)P(F) + P(flag|not F)P(not F)].

questions.statement: Trade sizes are right-skewed with standard deviation 30 shares. The standard error of the sample mean is computed from samples of n = 100. If the desk instead samples n = 400 independent trades, what happens to the standard error?

options.text: It stays at 3 because the population is skewed
It falls from 3 to 1.5, i.e., it is halved
It falls from 3 to 0.75, i.e., it is quartered

solution.explanation: SE = σ/√n: 30/10 = 3 for n = 100 and 30/20 = 1.5 for n = 400. Quadrupling n only halves SE. Skewness affects how fast the sampling distribution becomes normal, not the SE formula.

hints: Standard error = σ / √n. What does multiplying n by 4 do to √n?

questions.statement: With the sample size fixed, an analyst reduces the significance level from α = 0.05 to α = 0.01. What is the usual effect?

options.text: Type I error increases and power increases
Type I error rate decreases and Type II error rate increases (power decreases)
Neither changes unless the sample size changes
Both Type I and Type II error rates decrease

solution.explanation: A stricter α demands stronger evidence to reject H0: fewer false positives but more missed true effects (lower power) for a given n and effect size.

hints: A stricter α makes rejecting H0 harder: effect on false positives and on missed true effects?

questions.statement: In an A/B test, control converted 200 of 2,000 users (10%) and treatment 240 of 2,000 (12%). Using a pooled two-proportion z-test, what is the z statistic (approximately) and the conclusion at α = 0.05 (two-sided)?

options.text: z ≈ 2.02, so the difference is not significant because the critical value is 2.58
z ≈ 2.02, so the difference is statistically significant
z ≈ 0.02, so the difference is not significant
z ≈ 4.0, so the difference is significant

hints: z = (p₂ − p₁) / √(p̄(1 − p̄)(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)) with pooled p̄ = total conversions / total users.

questions.statement: In an ε-greedy bandit used to choose which alert-ranking model to show analysts, what does ε = 0.1 mean?

options.text: With probability 0.1 a random model is tried (exploration); otherwise the model with the best estimated reward is used (exploitation)
The best model is chosen 10% of the time and a random one 90%

solution.explanation: ε-greedy balances exploration and exploitation: exploit the best-known arm most of the time and explore a random arm with probability ε.

hints: ε is the probability of exploring (trying a random option).

questions.statement: What is the main purpose of a model card for a production ML model?

options.text: To store the model's weights and source code
To guarantee the model is unbiased
To document intended use, training/evaluation data, performance across groups, limitations and known risks so users can judge appropriate use

solution.explanation: Model cards support transparency and accountability by summarising context, metrics and limitations. They do not guarantee fairness and do not replace testing or monitoring.

hints: It documents intended use, data, performance and limitations.

questions.statement: A feed-forward network has three dense layers but every layer uses the identity (linear) activation. What is the effect on the function the network can represent?

options.text: It can approximate any continuous function because it has three layers
It is equivalent to a single linear transformation, so depth adds no representational power
It becomes equivalent to a decision tree of depth three
It can represent XOR because depth increases capacity

solution.explanation: Composition of linear maps is linear: W3(W2(W1x)) = (W3W2W1)x. Non-linear activations (ReLU, tanh, ...) are what let depth model non-linear patterns like XOR.

hints: A product of linear maps is itself a linear map — what does that say about depth without non-linearity?

questions.statement: In a two-player game search, alpha-beta pruning is applied to minimax. Which statement is true?

options.text: It increases the number of nodes explored but makes each cheaper
It returns an approximate value that can differ from minimax, trading accuracy for speed
It returns the same root value as plain minimax while potentially exploring fewer nodes
It only works if every node has exactly two children

solution.explanation: Alpha-beta only prunes branches that cannot influence the final decision, so the minimax value is unchanged; the savings depend on move ordering. It works for any branching factor.

hints: Does pruning change the final minimax value, or only the amount of work?

questions.statement: A team removes the protected attribute 'gender' from a credit model's inputs and claims the model is now unbiased. Why is that claim weak?

options.text: Other features (e.g., occupation or purchase categories) can act as proxies for gender, so disparities can persist; fairness must be measured on outcomes
Protected attributes are always the most predictive features, so removal is impossible
Fairness only matters for neural networks
Removing a feature can never change a model's predictions

solution.explanation: 'Fairness through unawareness' fails when other variables are correlated with the protected attribute. Auditing outcomes (e.g., approval and error rates by group) is required.

hints: Could other columns still carry the same information (proxies)?

solution.explanation: A subclass constructor implicitly calls `super()` first, so the superclass constructor body runs before the subclass constructor body.

hints: Which constructor body runs first: the superclass or the subclass?

questions.statement: You want every price row to appear together with the average close of its sector on the same row. Which construct achieves this without collapsing rows?

options.text: SELECT sector, AVG(close) ... GROUP BY sector

solution.explanation: Window aggregates compute a value over a partition but keep each input row. GROUP BY collapses rows to one per group.

hints: Which feature computes an aggregate over a partition WITHOUT collapsing rows?

questions.statement: A query lists every security with its filled trades: SELECT s.ticker, t.trade_id FROM Securities s LEFT JOIN Trades t ON t.security_id = s.security_id WHERE t.status = 'FILLED'. Securities that have no trades at all are missing from the output. Why?

options.text: LEFT JOIN only returns rows that have a match in both tables
The WHERE condition on the right-hand table is false (NULL) for the null-extended rows, so they are filtered out; the status test belongs in the ON clause
SQL removes NULL rows automatically after any join
Securities without trades violate a foreign-key constraint

solution.explanation: The WHERE clause is evaluated after the join; for unmatched securities t.status is NULL, and NULL = 'FILLED' is not true, so those rows disappear and the LEFT JOIN behaves like an INNER JOIN. Moving the predicate into ON preserves them.

hints: A WHERE condition on the right table of a LEFT JOIN removes the NULL-extended rows.

options.text: It does not compile because label() is not overridden

solution.explanation: `label()` is inherited, but the call `tag()` inside it is dispatched at run time on the actual object (a LimitOrder), so the overridden version runs. This is run-time polymorphism.

hints: Method calls inside the superclass are dispatched on the actual object type at run time.

questions.statement: A developer fixes a bug and re-runs the previously passing test suite to confirm nothing else broke. What is this called?

options.text: Acceptance testing by the end customer

solution.explanation: Regression testing re-executes existing tests after a change to make sure previously working behaviour has not been broken.

hints: Re-running existing tests after a change is called …?

questions.statement: A unit test for a function that computes a daily sentiment average calls a live sentiment API over the network. What is the best improvement?

options.text: Delete the test because networks are unreliable
Test only that the function does not throw an exception
Keep the live call and re-run the test until it passes
Replace the API with a stub/mock returning fixed values so the test is fast, deterministic and independent of the network

solution.explanation: Unit tests should isolate the unit under test. Stubbing the external dependency makes results repeatable, so assertions about the calculation are meaningful.

hints: How can you make a test fast and repeatable when it depends on the network?

questions.statement: A function returns the rolling mean of a series for a given window size. Which test is most likely to expose an off-by-one error in how the first rolling value is produced?

options.text: A test that checks only the data type of the return value
A series whose length equals the window size, expecting exactly one output equal to the mean of the whole series
A very long random series, checking only that the function does not crash
A series of identical values and a window of 1

solution.explanation: Edge cases at the boundary between 'not enough data' and 'one full window' reveal off-by-one mistakes. Long random inputs and type checks do not pin down the first index.

hints: Off-by-one bugs hide at the boundary: smallest input that still produces an output.

questions.statement: Esha is taller than Gita; Asha is taller than Esha. Who is the tallest?

solution.explanation: Chain the statements: Asha > Esha > Gita (tallest to shortest). The tallest is Asha.

hints: Arrange the people in a chain from the comparisons, then read off the requested position.

questions.statement: Ravi is 36 years old and his son is 14 years old. What will be the sum of their ages after 5 years?

solution.explanation: Each ages 5 years: 36+14+10 = 60.

hints: Every person's age increases by the same number of years.

questions.statement: In a group, 40 people like tea, 35 like coffee and 8 like both. How many like at least one of them?
The sum of two numbers is 8 and their difference is 2. Find the larger number.

solution.explanation: Larger = (sum + difference)/2 = 5.

hints: Larger = (sum + difference)/2.

questions.statement: 2 kg of rice at 30 per kg is mixed with 3 kg of rice at 50 per kg. What is the price per kg of the mixture?

solution.explanation: Total cost = 210; total weight = 5; mean price = 42.

hints: Mixture price = total cost / total quantity.

questions.statement: In how many ways can 3 different posts be chosen from 5 people if no person holds two posts? (Use 3 posts)

solution.explanation: Ordered selection: 5P3 = 60.

hints: Different posts means order matters: nPr = n!/(n − r)!.

questions.statement: A can do a piece of work in 6 days and B in 3 days. Working together, in how many days will they finish it?

solution.explanation: Combined rate = 1/6 + 1/3 = 9/18. Time = 18/9 = 2 days.

hints: Add the rates: 1/a + 1/b; time = 1 / combined rate.

questions.statement: What is 20% of 200 plus 10% of 500?

solution.explanation: 20% of 200 = 40 and 10% of 500 = 50; the sum is 90.

hints: Compute each percentage separately, then add.

questions.statement: Find the compound interest on 10000 at 10% per annum for 2 years, compounded annually.

solution.explanation: Amount = 10000×(1+10/100)² = 12100. CI = amount − principal = 2100.

hints: A = P(1 + r/100)^n and CI = A − P.

questions.statement: What is the smaller angle between the hour and minute hands of a clock at 6:00?

solution.explanation: Angle = |30h − 5.5m| = |180 − 0| = 180°; the smaller angle is 180°.

hints: Angle = |30h − 5.5m| degrees (take 360 minus it if it exceeds 180).

questions.statement: A bag has 3 red and 7 blue balls. Two balls are drawn one after another without replacement. What is the probability that both are red?
hints: Without replacement the second draw has one fewer ball of that colour and one fewer ball overall.

questions.statement: A shopkeeper marks an article at 1000 and gives a discount of 10%. If the cost price is 700, what is his profit percentage?
hints: First find the selling price after the discount, then profit % = (SP − CP)/CP × 100.

questions.statement: What is the last digit of 9^2011?

solution.explanation: Last digits of powers of 9 repeat with period 4: 9, 1, 9, 1. 2011 mod 4 = 3, giving 9.

hints: Last digits of powers repeat in a cycle (length at most 4); reduce the exponent mod the cycle length.

questions.statement: The average weight of 6 players is 30 kg. A player weighing 24 kg leaves and another weighing 40 kg joins. What is the new average?

solution.explanation: New total = 180 − 24 + 40 = 196; divide by 6: 32.67 kg.

hints: Replace the individual in the total, not in the average, then divide by the (unchanged) count.

questions.statement: Two numbers are in the ratio 2:3 and their sum is 60. If 10 is added to each, what is the new ratio (in simplest form)?

solution.explanation: Numbers are 24 and 36. After adding 10: 34:46 = 17:23.

hints: Find the actual numbers first, then add and simplify the ratio.

questions.title: January Purchases by Channel
questions.statement:
The payments team wants an overview of January 2025 spending per channel.

Using the `Transactions` table, consider only **purchases** (`amount > 0`) whose `txn_time` is in January 2025 (from `'2025-01-01 00:00:00'` up to but **not including** `'2025-02-01 00:00:00'`). For each `channel` that has **at least 2** such purchases return:

`channel, purchases, avg_amount`

* `purchases` – number of qualifying purchases
* `avg_amount` – average `amount`, rounded to 2 decimals

Sort by `avg_amount` descending, then `channel` ascending.

tables.name: Transactions
tables.description: Card/bank transactions; negative amounts are refunds.

questions.schemaSql:
CREATE TABLE Transactions (
  txn_id           INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  account_id       INTEGER NOT NULL,
  txn_time         TEXT NOT NULL,        -- 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS'
  amount           REAL NOT NULL,        -- negative = refund
  channel          TEXT NOT NULL,        -- 'POS', 'ONLINE' or 'ATM'
  merchant_country TEXT NOT NULL
);
questions.starterQuery:
SELECT channel, COUNT(*) AS purchases, ROUND(AVG(amount), 2) AS avg_amount
FROM Transactions
-- TODO: WHERE (purchases in January 2025), GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY
GROUP BY channel;
questions.outputSpec: Columns, in order: channel, purchases, avg_amount. Ordered by avg_amount DESC, channel ASC.

hiddenTests.description: No channel has two January purchases (empty result)

solution.referenceSolution:
SELECT channel,
       COUNT(*)              AS purchases,
       ROUND(AVG(amount), 2) AS avg_amount
FROM Transactions
WHERE amount > 0
  AND txn_time >= '2025-01-01 00:00:00'
  AND txn_time <  '2025-02-01 00:00:00'
GROUP BY channel
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY avg_amount DESC, channel ASC;
solution.explanation: Filter rows first (positive amounts in the half-open January window), group by channel, keep groups with HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2, then order. Using BETWEEN with a date-only upper bound would miss late-January times.

rubric.formula: earned = 100 * (sum of weights of passed tests) / (sum of all test weights)
rules: A submission that only compiles/executes without matching expected output earns 0 for that test.
A crash, syntax error or timeout fails only the affected test; remaining tests are still scored.
Half-open date range: 2025-02-01 00:00:00 must be excluded.
Refunds (negative amounts) are excluded before averaging.

questions.walkthrough: Purchases in January 2025 only: refunds (negative amounts), the 2024-12-31 trade and the trade at exactly 2025-02-01 00:00:00 are excluded. ONLINE has 4 qualifying purchases (980, 800, 150, 260) → average 547.50. POS has 7 purchases (120.50, 45.25, 15.75, 22.10, 70.00, 80.00 and 40.00) → average 56.23. ATM has only one purchase, so HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 removes it.
hints: Purchases are rows with amount > 0. Dates are text 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS', so they compare correctly as strings.
Use txn_time >= '2025-01-01 00:00:00' AND txn_time < '2025-02-01 00:00:00' — a half-open range includes all of 31 January.
GROUP BY channel, then HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2, ROUND(AVG(amount), 2) and the requested ORDER BY.

questions.title: January Spending of Active Accounts
questions.statement:
Compliance wants to review heavy January 2025 activity.

Join `Accounts` and `Transactions` and return, for every account whose `status = 'ACTIVE'`:

`account_id, customer_name, txn_count, total_amount, largest_txn`

Only count **purchases** (`amount > 0`; refunds are negative) made in January 2025, i.e. `txn_time` from `'2025-01-01 00:00:00'` up to but **excluding** `'2025-02-01 00:00:00'`. Return only accounts with **at least 3** such purchases. `total_amount` is `SUM(amount)` rounded to 2 decimals and `largest_txn` the maximum amount. Sort by `total_amount` descending, then `account_id` ascending.

tables.name: Transactions
tables.description: Card/bank transactions; negative amounts are refunds.

questions.schemaSql:
CREATE TABLE Accounts (
  account_id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_name TEXT NOT NULL,
  country       TEXT NOT NULL,
  open_date     TEXT NOT NULL,
  status        TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('ACTIVE','CLOSED','FROZEN'))
);
CREATE TABLE Transactions (
  txn_id           INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  account_id       INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES Accounts(account_id),
  txn_time         TEXT NOT NULL,        -- 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS'
  amount           REAL NOT NULL,        -- negative = refund
  channel          TEXT NOT NULL,
  merchant_country TEXT NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE AccountProfiles (
  account_id         INTEGER PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES Accounts(account_id),
  risk_tier          TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (risk_tier IN ('LOW','MEDIUM','HIGH')),
  avg_monthly_spend  REAL,               -- NULL when unknown
  home_country       TEXT NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE RiskAlerts (
  alert_id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  txn_id     INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES Transactions(txn_id),
  alert_type TEXT NOT NULL,
  severity   TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (severity IN ('LOW','MEDIUM','HIGH','CRITICAL')),
  created_at TEXT NOT NULL,
  resolved   INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (resolved IN (0,1))
);
questions.starterQuery:
SELECT a.account_id, a.customer_name, COUNT(*) AS txn_count, 0.0 AS total_amount, 0.0 AS largest_txn
FROM Accounts a
JOIN Transactions t ON t.account_id = a.account_id
-- TODO: filters, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY
;
questions.outputSpec: Columns, in order: account_id, customer_name, txn_count, total_amount, largest_txn. Order: total_amount DESC, account_id ASC.

hiddenTests.description: Equal totals -> tie broken by account_id

solution.referenceSolution:
SELECT a.account_id, a.customer_name,
       COUNT(*)                    AS txn_count,
       ROUND(SUM(t.amount), 2)     AS total_amount,
       MAX(t.amount)               AS largest_txn
FROM Accounts a
JOIN Transactions t ON t.account_id = a.account_id
WHERE a.status = 'ACTIVE'
  AND t.txn_time >= '2025-01-01 00:00:00' AND t.txn_time < '2025-02-01 00:00:00'
  AND t.amount > 0
GROUP BY a.account_id, a.customer_name
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
ORDER BY total_amount DESC, a.account_id ASC;
solution.explanation: Filter before grouping (status, half-open date range, amount > 0), group per account and apply HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3. A BETWEEN '2025-01-01' AND '2025-01-31' filter would miss late-January timestamps.

rubric.formula: earned = 200 * (sum of weights of passed tests) / (sum of all test weights)
rules: A submission that only compiles/executes without matching expected output earns 0 for that test.
A crash, syntax error or timeout fails only the affected test; remaining tests are still scored.
Refunds must be excluded before counting.

questions.walkthrough: Account 1 (ACTIVE) has purchases of 120.50, 980.00 and 45.25 in January → 3 purchases, total 1,145.75, largest 980.00. Its refund (−30.00) and the 2025-02-01 00:00:00 trade are excluded. Account 2 has 310.00 + 15.75 + 22.10 = 347.85. Account 3 is CLOSED and account 5 FROZEN. Account 4 has only 2 January purchases (the 2024-12-31 one is outside the month).
hints: Only ACTIVE accounts and only purchases in the half-open January window should be counted — do this filtering in WHERE.
JOIN Accounts to Transactions on account_id, then GROUP BY the account so each row summarises one account.
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 is wrong here — the spec says at least 3 purchases. Finish with ROUND(SUM(amount), 2), MAX(amount) and ORDER BY total_amount DESC, account_id.

questions.title: Calendar Features from Timestamps
questions.statement:
Create calendar features from transaction timestamps.

1. Parse `txn_time` with format `%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S`; drop rows that cannot be parsed.
2. Add `date` (the timestamp at midnight, datetime), `weekday` (English day name such as `Saturday`), `is_weekend` (Saturday or Sunday), `month` (text like `2025-03`) and `hour` (0–23, int64).
3. Sort by `txn_time`, then `txn_id`; return `txn_id, txn_time, date, weekday, is_weekend, month, hour` with a fresh index.
questions.starterCode:
import pandas as pd

def calendar_features(txns: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    df = txns.copy()

solution.referenceSolution:
import pandas as pd

def wide_returns(returns):
    df = returns.copy()
    df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"])
    wide = df.pivot_table(index="date", columns="symbol", values="ret", aggfunc="mean", dropna=False)
    wide = wide.reindex(sorted(wide.columns), axis=1)
    out = wide.copy()
    out["market_avg"] = wide.mean(axis=1, skipna=True)
    out["n_reporting"] = wide.notna().sum(axis=1).astype("int64")
    out = out.sort_index().reset_index()
    out.columns.name = None
    return out
solution.explanation: pivot_table with aggfunc='mean' collapses duplicates; dropna=False keeps all-NaN cells. Mean with skipna handles missing symbols; notna().sum(axis=1) counts reporting symbols.

solution.referenceSolution:
import pandas as pd

def running_stats(daily):
    df = daily.copy()
    df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"])
    df = df.sort_values(["symbol", "date"], kind="mergesort").reset_index(drop=True)
    g = df.groupby("symbol")["volume"]
    df["vol_ma3"] = g.transform(lambda s: s.rolling(3, min_periods=1).mean())
    df["cum_volume"] = g.cumsum()
    df["volume_rank"] = g.rank(method="min", ascending=False).astype("int64")
    return df[["symbol", "date", "volume", "vol_ma3", "cum_volume", "volume_rank"]]
solution.explanation: Sort first, then use groupby on the symbol: transform with rolling(3, min_periods=1).mean(), cumsum() and rank(method='min', ascending=False) all stay aligned with the sorted rows.

import pandas as pd

def risk_summary(txns):
    df = txns.dropna(subset=["amount"]).copy()
    df["night_amount"] = df["amount"].where(df["is_night"], 0.0)
    out = (df.groupby("account_id", as_index=False)
             .agg(n_txn=("amount", "size"), total_amount=("amount", "sum"), max_amount=("amount", "max"),

    out = out[out["n_txn"] >= 2]
    return out.sort_values(["total_amount", "account_id"], ascending=[False, True]).reset_index(drop=True)

solution.referenceSolution:
import heapq
from typing import List
from collections import defaultdict

def top_k_entities(events: List[List], k: int) -> List[str]:
    total = defaultdict(int)
    for name, weight in events:
        total[name] += weight
    best = heapq.nsmallest(k, total.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))
    return [name for name, _ in best]
solution.explanation: Aggregate totals in a hash map, then select the k best with a heap (heapq.nsmallest with key (-total, name)). The key encodes both the ordering and the tie-break.
